stemMd: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

options.label: A
options.textMd: It describes a long-standing problem in geology and then proposes a solution that has yet to be tried.

options.label: B
options.textMd: It opens with a surprising measurement and then traces, step by step, the chain of events that produced it.

options.label: C
options.textMd: It introduces a dating method, explains the principle it rests on, and then reports a test that showed both its usefulness and its limit.

options.label: D
options.textMd: It contrasts two competing ways of dating rockfalls and argues that one of them has been made obsolete.

explanationMd:
Structure questions are answered by labelling each sentence's job, not by recalling content.

Sentence 1 sets the scene (bare stone after a fall). Sentence 2 introduces the method (widest lichen gives a minimum age). Sentence 3 names the test (boulders below a cliff with dated collapses). Sentences 4 and 5 give the two-sided outcome: close agreement under about 300 years, blurring beyond it. Labelled in order, that is introduce, explain, test, qualify — which is Choice A.

A fast way to check: read only the first and last sentences. The text starts with bare rock and ends with a limitation on the method, so any option that ends somewhere else — with a comparison won, a solution proposed, or a chain of causes — has the wrong shape.

distractorRationale.d: Only one dating method is described. Parish registers appear as the yardstick the method is measured against, and nothing in the text is called obsolete.
distractorRationale.a: The order is reversed and the test is erased. The method is introduced before any difficulty is mentioned, and the text reports a test that has already been carried out rather than proposing an untried idea.
distractorRationale.b: No measurement opens the text, and nothing surprising is announced. The numbers appear at the end, as the outcome of the test rather than as the puzzle the text sets out to explain.
